problems.title: Acceleration points back to equilibrium
problems.objective: Analyze acceleration points back to equilibrium with an explicit physical model, consistent signs and SI units, and a limiting or sanity check.
problems.statement: A cart executes simple harmonic motion along the $x$ axis with equilibrium at $x=0$. At one instant $x=+0.080\,\mathrm m$ and $\omega=5.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. Find its acceleration and state its direction.
problems.strategy: First: Use the SHM relation $a=-\omega^2x$. Next: Substitute the signed displacement rather than its magnitude alone. Finally: Check that the acceleration points toward equilibrium and has units of $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

commonErrors.consequence: The resulting acceleration points away from equilibrium and cannot produce stable SHM.

commonErrors.description: Adds a constant $g$ term after measuring from static equilibrium.

problems.solution: With downward positive, $m\ddot y=mg-k(\Delta_0+y)$. Since $mg=k\Delta_0$, this becomes $m\ddot y=-ky$, so $\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}$. Gravity shifts equilibrium but does not change the ideal linear frequency.

problems.statement: A disk of rotational inertia $I=0.0200\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ is suspended by a wire with torsional constant $\kappa=0.500\,\mathrm{N\,m/rad}$. For small twists, find its angular frequency and period.
problems.strategy: First: Use the restoring torque $\tau=-\kappa\theta$. Next: Match $I\ddot\theta+\kappa\theta=0$ to SHM. Finally: Compute $T=2\pi\sqrt{I/\kappa}$ and check units.
hints: Use the restoring torque $\tau=-\kappa\theta$.

Executes the decisive calculation or derivation: Match $I\ddot\theta+\kappa\theta=0$ to SHM.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Compute $T=2\pi\sqrt{I/\kappa}$ and check units.

commonErrors.description: Inverts the torsional-oscillator ratio and uses $\omega_0=\sqrt{I/\kappa}$.
commonErrors.consequence: The angular equation gives $\omega_0^2=\kappa/I$; reversing the ratio gives wrong dimensions and period.

commonErrors.description: Treats radians as an additional physical dimension.
commonErrors.consequence: Radians are dimensionless, leaving $\kappa/I$ with units $\mathrm{s^{-2}}$.

problems.solution: $\omega_0=\sqrt{\kappa/I}=\sqrt{0.500/0.0200}=5.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ and $T=2\pi/5.00=1.26\,\mathrm s$.
problems.flawedProof: $\omega_0=\sqrt{I/\kappa}=0.200\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, so $T=31.4\,\mathrm s$.

problems.title: Parameters of an underdamped oscillator
problems.objective: Analyze parameters of an underdamped oscillator with an explicit physical model, consistent signs and SI units, and a limiting or sanity check.
problems.statement: A damped oscillator obeys $m\ddot x+b\dot x+kx=0$ with $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $b=2.00\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, and $k=25.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$. Classify the damping and find the decay constant and damped angular frequency.
problems.strategy: First: Compute $\gamma=b/(2m)$ and $\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}$. Next: Compare $\gamma$ with $\omega_0$. Finally: Use $\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\gamma^2}$ and retain inverse-second units.

commonErrors.description: Uses $b/m$ as the amplitude decay constant.
commonErrors.consequence: The underdamped envelope is $e^{-bt/(2m)}$, so this doubles the decay rate.

commonErrors.description: Adds $\gamma^2$ when computing $\omega_d$.
commonErrors.consequence: Damping lowers the oscillation frequency below $\omega_0$.

problems.solution: $\gamma=1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $\omega_0=5.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, so the motion is underdamped. $\omega_d=\sqrt{25-1}=4.90\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
problems.flawedProof: $\gamma=b/m=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Using $\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\gamma^2}$ then gives $\omega_d=\sqrt{25-4}=4.58\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

problems.strategy: First: Compute $\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}$. Next: Use $Q=m\omega_0/b$ for viscous light damping. Finally: Interpret a value much larger than one as a relatively sharp resonance.

problems.title: Damped resonance frequency
problems.objective: Analyze damped resonance frequency with an explicit physical model, consistent signs and SI units, and a limiting or sanity check.
problems.statement: For a driven displacement response with $\omega_0=20.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ and damping constant $\gamma=b/(2m)=3.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, find the frequency at which displacement amplitude is maximal. State the condition under which this nonzero resonance exists.
problems.strategy: First: Use $\omega_r=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-2\gamma^2}$ for displacement resonance. Next: Evaluate the radicand before taking the root. Finally: State that the radicand must be positive.
permittedResults: For viscous displacement resonance, $\omega_r^2=\omega_0^2-2\gamma^2$ when positive.

commonErrors.description: Identifies the peak exactly at $\omega_0$ despite finite damping.
commonErrors.consequence: Viscous damping shifts the displacement-amplitude peak below the natural frequency.

commonErrors.description: Ignores a negative radicand in strongly damped cases.
commonErrors.consequence: A real nonzero resonance frequency does not exist unless $\omega_0^2>2\gamma^2$.

problems.solution: $\omega_r=\sqrt{400-18}=19.5\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. A nonzero displacement-resonance peak requires $\omega_0^2>2\gamma^2$; otherwise the response decreases from zero frequency.

problems.title: Derive the ideal SHM trajectory
problems.objective: Analyze derive the ideal shm trajectory with an explicit physical model, consistent signs and SI units, and a limiting or sanity check.
problems.statement: Starting from $\ddot x+\omega_0^2x=0$ with $\omega_0>0$, derive the real solution satisfying $x(0)=x_0$ and $\dot x(0)=v_0$. Then verify it directly in the differential equation.
problems.strategy: First: Solve the constant-coefficient characteristic equation or use sine and cosine basis functions. Next: Apply the two initial conditions to determine both constants. Finally: Differentiate twice and substitute to verify the equation and units.
permittedResults: The real solutions associated with roots $\pm i\omega_0$ are linear combinations of sine and cosine.
hints: Solve the constant-coefficient characteristic equation or use sine and cosine basis functions.
Apply the two initial conditions to determine both constants.
Differentiate twice and substitute to verify the equation and units.

Executes the decisive calculation or derivation: Apply the two initial conditions to determine both constants.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Differentiate twice and substitute to verify the equation and units.

commonErrors.description: Uses only a cosine term for arbitrary initial data.
commonErrors.consequence: One free constant cannot satisfy both independent displacement and velocity conditions.

commonErrors.description: Writes the sine coefficient as $v_0\omega_0$.
commonErrors.consequence: Differentiation shows it must be $v_0/\omega_0$ to match velocity units.

problems.solution: The real general solution is $x=C\cos\omega_0t+D\sin\omega_0t$. From $x(0)=x_0$ and $\dot x(0)=v_0$, $C=x_0$ and $D=v_0/\omega_0$. Hence $x=x_0\cos\omega_0t+(v_0/\omega_0)\sin\omega_0t$. Twice differentiating gives $\ddot x=-\omega_0^2x$.
problems.flawedProof: The solution is $x=x_0\cos\omega_0t$. It satisfies the equation and $x(0)=x_0$, so it is the unique solution for every stated $v_0$.

problems.title: Prove conservation of ideal oscillator energy
problems.objective: Analyze prove conservation of ideal oscillator energy with an explicit physical model, consistent signs and SI units, and a limiting or sanity check.
problems.statement: Let $x(t)$ satisfy $m\ddot x+kx=0$ with $m,k>0$. Prove directly that $E(t)=\tfrac12m\dot x^2+\tfrac12kx^2$ is constant, and explain why this proof fails unchanged when a term $b\dot x$ is added.
problems.strategy: First: Differentiate $E(t)$ using the chain rule. Next: Factor $\dot x(m\ddot x+kx)$ and use the equation of motion. Finally: Repeat with damping to identify the negative power term.
permittedResults: The equation of motion may be substituted pointwise.
hints: Differentiate $E(t)$ using the chain rule.
Factor $\dot x(m\ddot x+kx)$ and use the equation of motion.
Repeat with damping to identify the negative power term.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the physical model and conventions correctly: Differentiate $E(t)$ using the chain rule.
Executes the decisive calculation or derivation: Factor $\dot x(m\ddot x+kx)$ and use the equation of motion.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Repeat with damping to identify the negative power term.

commonErrors.description: Claims each kinetic and potential term is separately constant.
commonErrors.consequence: Only their sum is conserved; the two terms exchange energy during a cycle.

commonErrors.description: Sets $\dot E=-b\dot x$ in the damped case.
commonErrors.consequence: Damping power is force times velocity, $-b\dot x^2$.

problems.solution: $\dot E=m\dot x\ddot x+kx\dot x=\dot x(m\ddot x+kx)=0$, so $E$ is constant. With $m\ddot x+b\dot x+kx=0$, the same calculation gives $\dot E=-b\dot x^2\le0$, not zero.
problems.flawedProof: Because no external force appears, both $\tfrac12m\dot x^2$ and $\tfrac12kx^2$ are separately constant. Therefore their sum is conserved.

problems.title: Quantify the small angle approximation
problems.objective: Analyze quantify the small angle approximation with an explicit physical model, consistent signs and SI units, and a limiting or sanity check.
problems.statement: For a pendulum released at angular amplitude $\theta_0=0.200\,\mathrm{rad}$, estimate the maximum fractional error made by replacing $\sin\theta$ with $\theta$ using the first neglected Taylor term. Does the linear model overestimate or underestimate the restoring-torque magnitude?
problems.strategy: First: Use $\sin\theta=\theta-\theta^3/6+O(\theta^5)$. Next: Divide the leading absolute error $\theta^3/6$ by $|\theta|$. Finally: Use $|\sin\theta|<|\theta|$ for nonzero amplitudes below $\pi$ to determine the direction of error.
hints: Use $\sin\theta=\theta-\theta^3/6+O(\theta^5)$.
Divide the leading absolute error $\theta^3/6$ by $|\theta|$.
Use $|\sin\theta|<|\theta|$ for nonzero amplitudes below $\pi$ to determine the direction of error.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the physical model and conventions correctly: Use $\sin\theta=\theta-\theta^3/6+O(\theta^5)$.
Executes the decisive calculation or derivation: Divide the leading absolute error $\theta^3/6$ by $|\theta|$.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Use $|\sin\theta|<|\theta|$ for nonzero amplitudes below $\pi$ to determine the direction of error.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\theta_0^3/6$ itself as a fractional error.
commonErrors.consequence: A fractional comparison requires division by the retained linear term $|\theta_0|$.

commonErrors.description: Claims the approximation underestimates the torque.
commonErrors.consequence: For the stated range, the linear term is larger in magnitude than the sine.

problems.solution: The leading fractional error relative to the linear term is $\theta_0^2/6=(0.200)^2/6=6.67\times10^{-3}$, or about $0.667\%$. Since $|\sin\theta|<|\theta|$, the linear model slightly overestimates the restoring-torque magnitude.
problems.flawedProof: The fractional error is the first omitted term itself: $\theta_0^3/6=0.00133$, or $0.133\%$. The linear approximation therefore overestimates the exact torque by about that fraction.

problems.title: Block restored by springs on both sides
problems.objective: Analyze block restored by springs on both sides with an explicit physical model, consistent signs and SI units, and a limiting or sanity check.
problems.statement: A block of mass $m=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ lies on a frictionless line between two relaxed springs fixed to opposite walls. For a small displacement $x$ to the right, the left and right spring constants are $k_L=30.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$ and $k_R=50.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$. Find the net restoring force and oscillation period.
problems.strategy: First: Track how the displacement stretches one spring and compresses the other. Next: Add their restoring forces with signs. Finally: Use the resulting $k_{\mathrm{eff}}$ in the period and check that both springs stiffen the motion.
hints: Track how the displacement stretches one spring and compresses the other.
Add their restoring forces with signs.
Use the resulting $k_{\mathrm{eff}}$ in the period and check that both springs stiffen the motion.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the physical model and conventions correctly: Track how the displacement stretches one spring and compresses the other.
Executes the decisive calculation or derivation: Add their restoring forces with signs.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Use the resulting $k_{\mathrm{eff}}$ in the period and check that both springs stiffen the motion.

commonErrors.description: Subtracts the spring constants because the springs lie on opposite sides.
commonErrors.consequence: Their forces oppose the displacement in the same direction and therefore add.

commonErrors.description: Treats the arrangement as series springs.
commonErrors.consequence: The block displacement changes both springs directly; they do not carry a common transmitted force in series.

problems.solution: A rightward displacement makes each spring exert a leftward force, so $F_x=-(k_L+k_R)x=-80.0x\,\mathrm N$. Thus $T=2\pi\sqrt{2.00/80.0}=0.993\,\mathrm s$.
problems.flawedProof: The springs pull oppositely, so $F_x=-(k_R-k_L)x=-20.0x$ and $T=2\pi\sqrt{2.00/20.0}=1.99\,\mathrm s$.

problems.title: Rolling cylinder oscillates in a circular track
problems.objective: Analyze rolling cylinder oscillates in a circular track with an explicit physical model, consistent signs and SI units, and a limiting or sanity check.
problems.statement: A uniform solid cylinder of radius $r=0.100\,\mathrm m$ rolls without slipping inside a circular track of radius $R=0.500\,\mathrm m$. For small angular displacement $\theta$ of its center from the bottom, derive the angular frequency and evaluate it using $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Use $I_{\mathrm{cm}}=mr^2/2$.
problems.strategy: First: Use arc coordinate $s=(R-r)\theta$ and rolling speed $v=r\Omega$. Next: Combine translational and rotational kinetic energy into an effective factor $m+I_{\mathrm{cm}}/r^2$. Finally: Linearize the gravitational restoring term and check the no-rotation limit.
hints: Use arc coordinate $s=(R-r)\theta$ and rolling speed $v=r\Omega$.
Combine translational and rotational kinetic energy into an effective factor $m+I_{\mathrm{cm}}/r^2$.
Linearize the gravitational restoring term and check the no-rotation limit.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the physical model and conventions correctly: Use arc coordinate $s=(R-r)\theta$ and rolling speed $v=r\Omega$.
Executes the decisive calculation or derivation: Combine translational and rotational kinetic energy into an effective factor $m+I_{\mathrm{cm}}/r^2$.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Linearize the gravitational restoring term and check the no-rotation limit.

commonErrors.description: Omits rotational kinetic energy.
commonErrors.consequence: That makes the effective inertia too small and overestimates the frequency.

commonErrors.description: Uses the center path radius $R$ instead of $R-r$.
commonErrors.consequence: The cylinder center travels on a circle of radius $R-r$.

problems.solution: The kinetic energy is $K=\tfrac12[m+I/r^2](R-r)^2\dot\theta^2=\tfrac34m(R-r)^2\dot\theta^2$. Also $U\approx\tfrac12mg(R-r)\theta^2$. Hence $\omega^2=mg(R-r)/[(m+I/r^2)(R-r)^2]=2g/[3(R-r)]$. Numerically $\omega=\sqrt{19.62/1.20}=4.04\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
problems.flawedProof: Ignore rotational kinetic energy and treat the center as a sliding point mass on radius $R-r$. Then $\omega=\sqrt{g/(R-r)}=4.95\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

commonErrors.description: Adds amplitudes arithmetically to get $7.00\,\mathrm{cm}$.

problems.solution: $x=3.00\cos\omega t-4.00\sin\omega t$ in centimetres. Thus $A\cos\phi=3.00$ and $A\sin\phi=4.00$, giving $A=5.00\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $\phi=\tan^{-1}(4/3)=0.927\,\mathrm{rad}$.

problems.title: Beat envelope from nearby frequencies

problems.objective: Analyze pressure and displacement nodes in a pipe with an explicit physical model, consistent signs and SI units, and a limiting or sanity check.
problems.statement: An ideal pipe of length $L$ is closed at $x=0$ and open at $x=L$. For its fundamental acoustic mode, locate displacement nodes and antinodes and pressure nodes and antinodes. Explain why the two patterns are interchanged.
problems.strategy: First: Apply zero normal air motion at the rigid closed end. Next: Apply approximately atmospheric pressure fluctuation zero at the open end. Finally: Use pressure fluctuation proportional to the spatial derivative of displacement.
permittedResults: A rigid end is a displacement node; an ideal open end is a pressure node.
Acoustic pressure fluctuation is proportional to minus the displacement gradient.
hints: Apply zero normal air motion at the rigid closed end.
Apply approximately atmospheric pressure fluctuation zero at the open end.
Use pressure fluctuation proportional to the spatial derivative of displacement.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the physical model and conventions correctly: Apply zero normal air motion at the rigid closed end.
Executes the decisive calculation or derivation: Apply approximately atmospheric pressure fluctuation zero at the open end.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Use pressure fluctuation proportional to the spatial derivative of displacement.

commonErrors.description: Places pressure and displacement nodes at the same locations.
commonErrors.consequence: Pressure depends on compression, hence displacement gradient, so their node patterns are complementary.

commonErrors.description: Calls the open end a displacement node.
commonErrors.consequence: Air can move most freely at an ideal open end, producing a displacement antinode.

problems.solution: For the fundamental, displacement has a node at $x=0$ and antinode at $x=L$. Pressure has an antinode at $x=0$ and node at $x=L$. Where displacement amplitude is extremal its spatial derivative vanishes, giving a pressure node; where displacement is constrained to zero its gradient and pressure amplitude can be maximal.
problems.flawedProof: Both pressure and displacement must vanish at the closed end because the air cannot move there, and both are maximal at the open end.

problems.title: Acoustic impedance matching at an interface
problems.objective: Analyze acoustic impedance matching at an interface with an explicit physical model, consistent signs and SI units, and a limiting or sanity check.
problems.statement: A normally incident plane sound wave crosses from medium 1 with acoustic impedance $Z_1=400\,\mathrm{Pa\,s/m}$ into medium 2 with $Z_2=1600\,\mathrm{Pa\,s/m}$. Find the pressure-amplitude reflection and transmission ratios and the reflected and transmitted intensity fractions.
problems.strategy: First: Use pressure coefficients $r_p=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_2+Z_1)$ and $t_p=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$. Next: Square the reflection coefficient for reflected intensity. Finally: Include the impedance ratio for transmitted intensity and verify energy conservation.
hints: Use pressure coefficients $r_p=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_2+Z_1)$ and $t_p=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$.
Square the reflection coefficient for reflected intensity.
Include the impedance ratio for transmitted intensity and verify energy conservation.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the physical model and conventions correctly: Use pressure coefficients $r_p=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_2+Z_1)$ and $t_p=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$.
Executes the decisive calculation or derivation: Square the reflection coefficient for reflected intensity.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Include the impedance ratio for transmitted intensity and verify energy conservation.

commonErrors.description: Sets transmitted intensity fraction to $t_p^2=2.56$.
commonErrors.consequence: Pressure amplitude alone does not determine power across different impedances.

commonErrors.description: Uses a negative reflection coefficient for entry into higher impedance.
commonErrors.consequence: Pressure reflects without inversion when $Z_2>Z_1$.

problems.solution: $r_p=(1600-400)/2000=0.600$ and $t_p=3200/2000=1.60$. Thus $R=r_p^2=0.360$ and $\mathcal T=(400/1600)(1.60)^2=0.640$. Their sum is one; pressure amplitude can exceed the incident value without transmitted power exceeding it.
problems.flawedProof: $R=r_p^2=0.360$ and $\mathcal T=t_p^2=(1.60)^2=2.56$. The sum exceeds one because pressure amplitude was treated directly as an intensity amplitude across both media.

problems.title: Uniform wind is not automatically a Doppler shift
problems.objective: Analyze uniform wind is not automatically a doppler shift with an explicit physical model, consistent signs and SI units, and a limiting or sanity check.
problems.statement: A source and observer are both fixed to the ground on a straight line while uniform wind of speed $u$ blows from source to observer. The source emits frequency $f$ in air whose sound speed relative to the air is $c$. Neglect gradients. Determine the frequency heard by the ground-fixed observer and explain why replacing $c$ by $c+u$ in only one part of a Doppler formula is wrong.
problems.strategy: First: Work in the ground frame to find the downwind crest speed $c+u$. Next: Find crest spacing from the distance advanced during one source period. Finally: Divide observer-relative crest speed by that same wavelength.
permittedResults: Frequency is crest encounter rate; uniform medium flow advects both speed and wavelength.
hints: Work in the ground frame to find the downwind crest speed $c+u$.
Find crest spacing from the distance advanced during one source period.
Divide observer-relative crest speed by that same wavelength.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the physical model and conventions correctly: Work in the ground frame to find the downwind crest speed $c+u$.
Executes the decisive calculation or derivation: Find crest spacing from the distance advanced during one source period.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Divide observer-relative crest speed by that same wavelength.

commonErrors.description: Uses $f'=f(c+u)/c$.
commonErrors.consequence: That changes the propagation speed but incorrectly keeps the no-wind wavelength.

commonErrors.description: Claims wind cannot affect wavelength.
commonErrors.consequence: It changes ground-frame crest spacing even though the encounter frequency remains the source frequency.

problems.solution: Successive crests move downwind at $c+u$, so their ground-frame spacing is $\lambda=(c+u)/f$. The stationary observer meets them at speed $c+u$, hence $f'=(c+u)/\lambda=f$. Uniform wind alone creates no Doppler shift when source and observer share the ground frame; changing speed without changing wavelength is inconsistent.
problems.flawedProof: Wind increases sound speed to $c+u$ while wavelength stays $c/f$, so the observer hears $f'=f(c+u)/c$.

problems.title: Unequal amplitude interference phasor
problems.objective: Analyze unequal amplitude interference phasor with an explicit physical model, consistent signs and SI units, and a limiting or sanity check.
problems.statement: At one point, two coherent harmonic contributions of the same frequency have displacement amplitudes $A$ and $2A$, with the second leading the first by $120^\circ$. Find the resultant amplitude and its phase relative to the first contribution. Give the intensity ratio to one contribution of amplitude $A$ in the same medium.
problems.strategy: First: Represent the first phasor as $A$ on the real axis and resolve the second into components. Next: Add components before taking magnitude and phase. Finally: Use intensity proportional to amplitude squared for the ratio.
permittedResults: Coherent harmonic amplitudes add as phasors.
At fixed medium and frequency, intensity is proportional to squared resultant amplitude.
hints: Represent the first phasor as $A$ on the real axis and resolve the second into components.
Add components before taking magnitude and phase.
Use intensity proportional to amplitude squared for the ratio.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the physical model and conventions correctly: Represent the first phasor as $A$ on the real axis and resolve the second into components.
Executes the decisive calculation or derivation: Add components before taking magnitude and phase.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Use intensity proportional to amplitude squared for the ratio.

commonErrors.description: Adds amplitudes to get $3A$ without phase resolution.
commonErrors.consequence: Non-collinear phasors do not add as positive scalar magnitudes.

commonErrors.description: Uses resultant amplitude ratio $\sqrt3$ as the intensity ratio.
commonErrors.consequence: Intensity is quadratic in amplitude.

problems.solution: $A+2A(\cos120^\circ+i\sin120^\circ)=A-A+i\sqrt3A=i\sqrt3A$. Thus the resultant amplitude is $\sqrt3A$ and it leads the first by $90^\circ$. The intensity ratio to a single amplitude-$A$ wave is $(\sqrt3A/A)^2=3$.
problems.flawedProof: The amplitudes add to $3A$ because both waves are present, so the intensity is nine times that of the amplitude-$A$ wave and the phase is $120^\circ$.

problems.title: Continuum limit and dispersive correction of a chain
problems.objective: Analyze continuum limit and dispersive correction of a chain with an explicit physical model, consistent signs and SI units, and a limiting or sanity check.
problems.statement: For the monatomic chain dispersion $\omega(k)=2\sqrt{K/m}\sin(ka/2)$ on small positive $k$, derive the continuum wave speed and the first dispersive correction through order $k^3$. Connect the result to the continuum equation obtained by Taylor expanding $u_{n\pm1}$.
problems.strategy: First: Expand the sine through its cubic term. Next: Factor the leading $ck$ and identify $c=a\sqrt{K/m}$. Finally: Taylor expand neighbor displacements to second order to recover $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ and interpret the next correction.
hints: Expand the sine through its cubic term.
Factor the leading $ck$ and identify $c=a\sqrt{K/m}$.
Taylor expand neighbor displacements to second order to recover $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ and interpret the next correction.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the physical model and conventions correctly: Expand the sine through its cubic term.
Executes the decisive calculation or derivation: Factor the leading $ck$ and identify $c=a\sqrt{K/m}$.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Taylor expand neighbor displacements to second order to recover $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ and interpret the next correction.

commonErrors.description: Claims the lattice is exactly nondispersive because the leading term is linear.
commonErrors.consequence: The cubic correction changes phase and group speeds at finite wavelength.

commonErrors.description: Gets a positive cubic correction from the sine expansion.
commonErrors.consequence: The cubic term of sine is negative, consistent with flattening toward the band edge.

problems.solution: $\omega=2\sqrt{K/m}[ka/2-(ka/2)^3/6+O(k^5a^5)]=ck[1-(ka)^2/24+O((ka)^4)]$, where $c=a\sqrt{K/m}$. The neighbor difference is $a^2u_{xx}+a^4u_{xxxx}/12+\cdots$, so $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}+(c^2a^2/12)u_{xxxx}+\cdots$. The leading equation is nondispersive; the higher spatial derivative produces the negative $k^3$ frequency correction.
problems.flawedProof: Keeping only $\sin(ka/2)\approx ka/2$ gives $\omega=ck$ exactly, so the chain is incorrectly declared nondispersive at every wavelength.

problems.title: String modes with a massive endpoint
problems.objective: Analyze string modes with a massive endpoint with an explicit physical model, consistent signs and SI units, and a limiting or sanity check.
problems.statement: A uniform string of length $L$, tension $T$, and density $\mu$ is fixed at $x=0$ and attached at $x=L$ to a point mass $M$ that moves transversely. Derive the normal-mode equation for wavenumber $k>0$. Check the limits $M\to0$ and $M\to\infty$ against free-end and fixed-end spectra.
problems.strategy: First: Use $X(x)=C\sin kx$ from the fixed boundary and $\omega=vk$ with $v^2=T/\mu$. Next: Apply Newton's law to the end mass using transverse string force $-TX'(L)$. Finally: Rearrange to a tangent equation and take both mass limits without dividing by a vanishing quantity incorrectly.
permittedResults: For small slope, the string force on the endpoint mass is $-T\partial_xy(L,t)$.
hints: Use $X(x)=C\sin kx$ from the fixed boundary and $\omega=vk$ with $v^2=T/\mu$.
Apply Newton's law to the end mass using transverse string force $-TX'(L)$.
Rearrange to a tangent equation and take both mass limits without dividing by a vanishing quantity incorrectly.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the physical model and conventions correctly: Use $X(x)=C\sin kx$ from the fixed boundary and $\omega=vk$ with $v^2=T/\mu$.
Executes the decisive calculation or derivation: Apply Newton's law to the end mass using transverse string force $-TX'(L)$.
States and checks the physical conclusion: Rearrange to a tangent equation and take both mass limits without dividing by a vanishing quantity incorrectly.

commonErrors.description: Imposes $X(L)=0$ for every finite endpoint mass.
commonErrors.consequence: A finite mass moves; its acceleration is balanced by the string slope force rather than a fixed displacement constraint.

commonErrors.description: Reverses the small- and large-mass limits.
commonErrors.consequence: A massless end has zero transverse force and behaves free, while an infinite mass cannot accelerate and behaves fixed.

problems.solution: With $y=X(x)\cos\omega t$ and $X=C\sin kx$, the mass equation is $-M\omega^2X(L)=-TX'(L)$. Thus $Tk\cos(kL)=M\omega^2\sin(kL)$. Using $\omega^2=(T/\mu)k^2$ gives $\tan(kL)=\mu/(Mk)$. As $M\to0$, the right side diverges and $kL\to(n+1/2)\pi$, the fixed-free spectrum. As $M\to\infty$, it tends to zero and $kL\to n\pi$, the fixed-fixed spectrum.
problems.flawedProof: The endpoint mass always makes the end fixed, so $X(L)=0$ and $kL=n\pi$ for every $M$. In the limit $M\to0$ the same fixed-end condition remains because the mass is still attached.
